full_judgment: Where the court acts without jurisdiction its 'error', 'omission' or 'irregularity' is not that of a Court of competent jurisdiction' rather such defect is that of a court which suffers from want of jurisdiction which cannot be cured under section 537 Criminal Procedure Code because the section has not made any reference to the finding, sentence and order of a court which has no jurisdiction. A decision of a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Bhola vs. Lachman, 1950 All, 475 supports the above view. Similar view has also been taken in the cases reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 690, AIR 1950 (All) 477 wherein it has been held by their Lordships that by invoking provisions of section 537 Criminal Procedure Code the defect of want of jurisdiction of a court in deciding a case cannot be cured. The aforesaid observations also supports my view that the provisions of section 537 Criminal Procedure Code cannot be taken in aid in the instant case to cure the defect of the impugned judgment of the court below which lacks in jurisdiction as the Sessions Judge had no jurisdiction in respect of the offence charged. Moreover, by invoking a provision of a procedure of a procedural law a court cannot be vested with jurisdiction ousting the provision of a substantive enactment which confers jurisdiction upon a court to decide a case. So viewed, section 537 Criminal Procedure Code being provision of a procedural law has no role to play in the instant case in order to cure the defect as to jurisdiction of the Sessions Judge in holding the trial of the present case. This point can also be looked into from another angle. Even if it is assumed that the Sessions Judge is clothed with the powers of Special Tribunal even then the judgment suffers from want of jurisdiction as it has no authority in law to try a scheduled offence like that of Article 4 (b) of the Ordinance and an offence under section 366A of the Penal Code because of joinder of a scheduled offence and a non-scheduled offence. The case of Talukder Abdul Aziz vs. State, 35 DLR, 127 supports the above view of mine wherein it has been held that joinder of scheduled and non-scheduled offences was illegal and also the cognizance by the Special Tribunal of both scheduled and non-scheduled offence was without jurisdiction. In Tamij Miah vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, 33 DLR 203, the same view was taken. Now let me consider the contention on section 29 of the Special Powers Act. It provides that the provisions of Criminal Procedure Code, so far only as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Special Powers Act. shall apply to the proceeding of Special Tribunals, and such Special Tribunals shall have all the powers conferred by the Code on a court of session exercising original jurisdiction. Section 29 has no manner of application where the provisions of Criminal Procedure Code are inconsistent with the provision of Special Powers Act. To put on interpretation that want of jurisdiction in taking cognizance of a scheduled offence of Special Tribunal Act by the Sessions Judge is cureable would be nothing but an absurd construction. In a clear and unambiguous language section 29 has made the provisions of Criminal Procedure Code applicable to a Special Tribunal and not to a Court of Sessions.
